events.statement: Across all services in the incident window 2026-06-01T14:00–15:30Z, exactly one deployment occurred: payment-service v6.0.0 (id dep-6203), deployed 2026-06-01T14:46:00Z by p.nair, summary 'New UPI mandate flow', changes 'mandate create/approve endpoints' and 'new ledger entry type MANDATE_HOLD', status 'rolled_back' with rolled_back_at 2026-06-01T15:12:00Z.

The deployment search over the wider pre-window 2026-06-01T08:00:00Z–16:59:00Z still returned only the single payment-service v6.0.0 deployment; no ledger-service, no shared-component, and no other service release exists in scope.
Config-change queries for 14:00–15:30Z and for the widened 08:00–16:59Z window both returned zero changes; no feature-flag or config change was recorded for any service around the onset.

payment-service's direct downstream graph is: payment-service -> ledger-db (kind 'db'), -> bank-partner-api (kind 'external', has_telemetry false), -> kafka (kind 'queue-produce'). ledger-db and kafka are marked shared:true.

ledger-db is a shared Postgres datastore with four other callers besides payment-service: order-service, portfolio-service, settlement-service (all 'db' edges), and it is reached via api-gateway -> order-service / portfolio-service / payment-service HTTP edges; so neighboring services can affect payment-service through the shared ledger-db.

Historical incident search returned 6 precedents; the two closest to 'ledger write failure' are HIST-114 (2025-04-18, ledger-db disk full from retained WAL, symptom 'write failures', root cause 'Inactive replication slot retained WAL until disk filled') and HIST-111 (2025-05-22, 'New report query without index did sequential scans'). None of the precedents cite a new ledger entry type or MANDATE_HOLD as a cause.

events.statement: payment-service v6.0.0 rollout completed at 2026-06-01T14:46:50Z ('deployment dep-6203 (v6.0.0) rollout complete, all pods ready'), ~14 minutes BEFORE the first payment error at 15:00:26Z. Errors therefore started AFTER the rollout completed, not during/after a 15:25Z onset.

First payment-service error is 2026-06-01T15:00:26Z; the ~15:25Z claim is wrong and the 15:10Z report is also ~10 min late. All 354 ERRORs match a single pattern: 'ledger write failed: ERROR: could not extend file: No space left on device', spanning 15:00:26Z to 16:57:54Z (gap in coverage between 15:00 and first_match).

payment-service error_rate jumped from a stable ~0.19-0.29% baseline (14:30-14:54Z, all max <=0.32) to avg 30.41% / max 60.8% in the 14:58-15:02Z bucket, then held ~60-65% through 16:58Z. The 240s bucketing means onset falls somewhere in 14:58-15:02Z; log granularity pins it to 15:00:26Z.

payment-service latency_p99_ms is flat across the whole window (baseline ~315-330ms, incident ~308-331ms; min 292.53, max 348.32) — NO latency anomaly. The failure is not a timeout/slowness symptom; requests fail fast.

ledger-db (the ledger writer's datastore — no 'ledger-service' exists) shows the CAUSE-side first: disk warning 'disk usage 95% on /var/lib/postgresql/data' at 14:15:45Z, 98% at 14:48:20Z, then first hard error at 15:01:01Z 'PANIC: could not write to file "pg_wal/xlogtemp.37478": No space left on device'. 292 ERRORs total; top patterns include 153 WAL PANICs and 139 'could not extend file "base/16402/2619"'. Also 'replication slot analytics_cdc is inactive; retaining 78423 MB of WAL' at 14:16:25Z.

Downstream-side confirmed: the payment-service error string is the verbatim PostgreSQL/DB error surfaced by the ledger writer, identical to ledger-db's own error class ('No space left on device'); DB disk saturation at ledger-db began ~45 min before payment errors and preceded them. payment-service has no 'restarts' or DB-pool metric anomaly needed — its error is a passthrough of the writer's storage failure.

events.answer: Onset of payment-service errors was 15:00:26Z — NOT ~15:25Z (the report's guess) and ~10 min before the 15:10Z report — and it occurred ~14 min AFTER the v6.0.0 rollout completed at 14:46:50Z, so errors began after rollout completion. The exact error signature is 'ledger write failed: ERROR: could not extend file: No space left on device' (354 hits, single pattern); error_rate went 0.2% → 60% in the 14:58-15:02Z bucket with flat p99 latency (~315ms). The failure is downstream-side: ledger-db (Postgres) hit 'No space left on device' — disk 95% at 14:15:45Z then 98% at 14:48:20Z, first write PANIC at 15:01:01Z, with an inactive replication slot 'analytics_cdc' retaining 78423 MB of WAL — and payment-service is merely surfacing the DB storage error.

events.statement: Independent change re-query for 14:30-15:30Z again returns exactly one change: payment-service v6.0.0 (dep-6203), deployed 2026-06-01T14:46:00Z, 'new ledger entry type MANDATE_HOLD', status 'rolled_back' with rolled_back_at 2026-06-01T15:12:00Z. No downstream/shared-service deployment exists in the window.

Config/flag changes for 14:00-15:30Z returned count 0, and deployments for the post-onset window 15:30-16:59Z also returned count 0 — so nothing was changed between the 15:12Z rollback and 16:59Z, i.e. the error rate stayed at ~60% for ~1h45m despite the rollback.

Change ordering relative to onset: v6.0.0 rollout completed 14:46:50Z, first payment error 15:00:26Z (+13m36s after deploy), rollback 15:12:00Z. The ledger-db disk warning pre-dates the deploy by ~31 min (14:15:45Z, 95%), so the resource-exhaustion signal leads the deployment, not the reverse.

Schema/support-change angle: no migration, config, feature-flag or ledger-side release was recorded anywhere in the incident window, so the new ledger entry type MANDATE_HOLD has no corresponding schema/config/support change in the inventory — the only artifact accompanying it is the payment-service code deploy itself. Whether MANDATE_HOLD is accepted by ledger-db cannot be tested, since the DB's failure mode (out-of-disk WAL) is entry-type-agnostic.

ledger-db is a shared Postgres with four caller services: order-service, portfolio-service, payment-service, settlement-service all hold 'db' edges to it (api-gateway -> order-service/portfolio-service/payment-service HTTP). Any of these neighbours can saturate the shared store and hurt payment-service via it.

Precedent check contradicts the described mechanism: HIST-114 (2025-04-18) has the identical symptom set ('no space left on device', 'write failures') and root cause 'Inactive replication slot retained WAL until disk filled', exactly matching the current ledger-db evidence — whereas no precedent (HIST-111/109/108/110/102) cites a new ledger entry type or mandate-flow change as a cause.

events.description: No migration/schema-change telemetry exists in the config/deploy tools for ledger-db, so I cannot prove or disprove that MANDATE_HOLD required a schema addition; the absence of any config change in tc-018/tc-010 is the only signal available.

I could not identify which shared-ledger-db caller workload (order/portfolio/settlement) or background process grew WAL/disk between 14:15:45Z and 15:01:01Z; no per-caller change was recorded and volume/WAL growth metrics were not queried by me.

events.answer: The true trigger is NOT payment-service v6.0.0 as a code-defect cause: it is the only change in the window (dep-6203, deployed 14:46:00Z/complete 14:46:50Z, rolled back 15:12:00Z), but it cannot explain the failure because the downstream/shared cause pre-dates it — ledger-db's disk was already 95% full at 14:15:45Z (31 min before the deploy) and its WAL/disk PANIC began at 15:01:01Z from an inactive replication slot retaining 78423 MB, exactly the HIST-114 precedent; payment-service's 'No space left on device' ledger-write error is a passthrough of that shared Postgres storage exhaustion. Competing candidates: (a) a missing ledger-side schema/support change for the new MANDATE_HOLD entry type — still standing only as unverifiable, since no schema/config/migration change existed anywhere in the window (zero config changes, zero other deployments) and the DB failure is entry-type-agnostic; (b) a neighbouring shared-ledger-db caller (order/portfolio/settlement) that accelerated disk/WAL growth — plausible but no corresponding change was recorded. v6.0.0 may at most be the workload that tipped an already-saturated DB over the edge, but it is not the root trigger.

events.title: Reporter's suspicion: v6.0.0 MANDATE_HOLD ledger entry type rejected by ledger-db (schema/validation mismatch)
ledger-db disk exhaustion from retained WAL (inactive replication slot) — storage-layer root cause independent of v6.0.0
Shared ledger-db saturated by a neighbouring caller (order/portfolio/settlement) writing excessive volume
Verdict: ledger-db volume at capacity / WAL backlog exhausted — cause-side resource exhaustion with v6.0.0 as coincidental timing

events.summary: The top hypothesis (H2/H4, same origin: ledger-db storage exhaustion from WAL retained by the inactive analytics_cdc replication slot) is well grounded at every hop and the alternatives are contradicted, not merely dismissed. Grounding: F11 is a direct ledger-db log observation of the 95%->98%->100% disk progression, the 'could not write to pg_wal/xlogtemp' PANIC, and the explicit 78423 MB retained-WAL message; F12/F8 show payment-service's error is the verbatim Postgres ENOSPC passthrough. Temporal order is established with the cause preceding onset by ~45 min (F15: disk warning 14:15:45Z vs first payment error 15:00:26Z; F7 pins rollout completion 14:46:50Z). Scope fits: the failure is entry-type-agnostic (F10 flat latency = fail-fast, F16 no schema/config/migration change anywhere), and F14 shows no recovery for ~1h45m after rollback with zero changes in 15:30-16:59Z. Alternatives: H1 restated in F13/F16 (the only change in the window is the rollback-independent passthrough), and H3 remains structurally unevidenced (its single hop was flagged by the automated check as evidence-free). Two gaps could in principle matter but the evidence needed to close them is either already observably absent or below the decisive threshold, so I accept rather than burn another round. Confidence capped at 0.85 to reflect that the disk-trend metric and per-caller write volume were never directly queried, and that 'the inactive slot is the dominant consumer' remains an inference from its size rather than a measured attribution.

events.why: top hypothesis is above threshold and clearly ahead

tasks.answer: The true trigger is NOT payment-service v6.0.0 as a code-defect cause: it is the only change in the window (dep-6203, deployed 14:46:00Z/complete 14:46:50Z, rolled back 15:12:00Z), but it cannot explain the failure because the downstream/shared cause pre-dates it — ledger-db's disk was already 95% full at 14:15:45Z (31 min before the deploy) and its WAL/disk PANIC began at 15:01:01Z from an inactive replication slot retaining 78423 MB, exactly the HIST-114 precedent; payment-service's 'No space left on device' ledger-write error is a passthrough of that shared Postgres storage exhaustion. Competing candidates: (a) a missing ledger-side schema/support change for the new MANDATE_HOLD entry type — still standing only as unverifiable, since no schema/config/migration change existed anywhere in the window (zero config changes, zero other deployments) and the DB failure is entry-type-agnostic; (b) a neighbouring shared-ledger-db caller (order/portfolio/settlement) that accelerated disk/WAL growth — plausible but no corresponding change was recorded. v6.0.0 may at most be the workload that tipped an already-saturated DB over the edge, but it is not the root trigger.

critiques.summary: The top hypothesis (H2/H4, same origin: ledger-db storage exhaustion from WAL retained by the inactive analytics_cdc replication slot) is well grounded at every hop and the alternatives are contradicted, not merely dismissed. Grounding: F11 is a direct ledger-db log observation of the 95%->98%->100% disk progression, the 'could not write to pg_wal/xlogtemp' PANIC, and the explicit 78423 MB retained-WAL message; F12/F8 show payment-service's error is the verbatim Postgres ENOSPC passthrough. Temporal order is established with the cause preceding onset by ~45 min (F15: disk warning 14:15:45Z vs first payment error 15:00:26Z; F7 pins rollout completion 14:46:50Z). Scope fits: the failure is entry-type-agnostic (F10 flat latency = fail-fast, F16 no schema/config/migration change anywhere), and F14 shows no recovery for ~1h45m after rollback with zero changes in 15:30-16:59Z. Alternatives: H1 restated in F13/F16 (the only change in the window is the rollback-independent passthrough), and H3 remains structurally unevidenced (its single hop was flagged by the automated check as evidence-free). Two gaps could in principle matter but the evidence needed to close them is either already observably absent or below the decisive threshold, so I accept rather than burn another round. Confidence capped at 0.85 to reflect that the disk-trend metric and per-caller write volume were never directly queried, and that 'the inactive slot is the dominant consumer' remains an inference from its size rather than a measured attribution.

challenges.issue: The disk-full attribution is inferred: no ledger-db disk_used_pct time series confirms the 95->98->100% progression, and 'the inactive slot (78423 MB) is the dominant consumer' is asserted from slot size rather than measured against total volume size. However, the retained-WAL message plus the WAL PANIC directly name the mechanism, so this is a sizing detail, not a different origin.

Whether MANDATE_HOLD would be rejected by a schema/validation layer is genuinely untestable (F16: no migration telemetry), and a ledger-db DDL applied out-of-band would be invisible to the change inventory. This is the one residual path to a different fix, but it is contradicted by the observed error class (storage ENOSPC, not constraint violation) and by F14 (errors persisted ~1h45m after rollback with zero post-rollback changes), so it is not blocking.

H3 has no evidence for its single causal hop (flagged by the automated check): no per-caller write/WAL volume metric was ever pulled, and payment-service's own v6.0.0 workload is never weighed as a candidate contributor to the growth between 14:15Z and 15:01Z. This is a real evidentiary hole, but H3 names the same origin as H2 (ledger-db disk exhaustion) and thus the same fix, so it does not change the ranking of the origin.

When H2 lists 'v6.0.0 may be the workload that tipped an already-saturated DB over the edge' it partially blurs the clean H2 claim. The origin is storage exhaustion either way, but the team should not later re-litigate the deploy as the cause; keep the origin statement about the ledger-db slot/volume.

Absence-of-change evidence (F2/F3/F13/F14) is being used to exclude a schema migration, but the dependency agent itself notes the migration data source does not exist, so this is inferring absence from an incomplete feed. This weakens the exclusion of H1 but does not rescue it, since the direct error-signature evidence (F8/F12) contradicts H1 independently.

H4 lists the identical supporting set as H2 and differs only in framing, which artificially inflates apparent corroboration. Treat them as one origin for confidence accounting rather than as two agreeing hypotheses.
